title: Why a slanting beam spreads out

sources.excerpt:
the light gets spread over larger and larger surface areas
more direct sunlight and to have longer days

Earth's tilted axis causes the seasons.
As the poles are on opposite ends of Earth, they experience opposite timing for the seasons.

claims.statement: The normal-incidence beam-and-ground illustration starts with a flat receiving patch perpendicular to the incoming beam.
Tilting a flat receiving surface beneath a fixed beam increases the illuminated footprint area.
The illustrated change in footprint is a geometric change at the receiver, without an increase or decrease in the incoming beam power.
The same beam power distributed over a larger receiving area supplies less energy per unit area.
At a fixed northern middle latitude, the winter local-noon Sun is lower than the summer local-noon Sun.
A more oblique beam has a broader footprint on the receiving surface; this applies to the seasonal noon-angle comparison at a fixed northern middle latitude.
Earth's tilted axis produces seasonal changes in the pattern of incoming sunlight angle as Earth travels around its orbit.
Earth's axial tilt also changes which hemisphere has longer days during the year.
The two hemispheres have opposite seasonal timing as they alternately tilt toward the incoming sunlight.

narration.text: Picture one fixed beam of light falling straight onto a flat patch of ground.
Now tilt the ground beneath it, and the same light spreads into a broader footprint.
Less energy reaches each small patch, although the beam itself has not become weaker.
At northern middle latitudes, winter's noon sunlight arrives lower and spreads wider than summer's.
Earth's tilted axis changes both sunlight angle and daylight length as the planet travels around its orbit.
The hemispheres take opposite turns toward the light, creating the familiar rhythm of summer and winter.

mustShow.text: A single straight-sided beam illuminates one flat ground patch viewed from a clear oblique camera angle.
Tilt the receiving ground beneath a beam whose width and direction stay fixed; its illuminated footprint visibly broadens.
Carry the same small set of symbolic light markers across the broader footprint, illustrating lower marker density without a numerical heat measurement.

At one fixed northern middle-latitude ground patch, compare local-noon winter and summer ray angles; the lower winter beam has a wider geometric footprint. Keep beam width, the ground patch and camera scale fixed; do not imply this comparison holds at every latitude or hour.
Show the same tilted Earth axis through orbital positions and daylight arcs, illustrating changing solar angle and day length.
Show the two hemispheres alternating toward the light as orbital position changes, with understated opposite seasonal landscape cues.

mustNotShow.text: Written labels, equations, watermarks, logos or text inside the generated shot art; this does not prohibit final engine-burned narration captions.
Recognizable real people, celebrity likenesses, NASA insignia or an implication of institutional endorsement.
Light rays bending because the receiving surface tilts, or a brighter source being used to explain the broader footprint.

style.text: Original editorial science illustration: cream, ink, cobalt and restrained teal, clean solid forms and calm camera motion. Begin with a tangible beam-and-ground demonstration before the planetary view. Straight parallel light rays and a consistently oriented Earth axis carry the geometry. The light markers are an illustrative convention, not measured temperatures or a physical simulation. No source artwork, branded assets, faces, logos, in-shot writing, quizzes or inferred learning claims. Keep all six narration beats visually distinct; final captions are produced by the engine. Claims are beat-specific: each criterion binds a claim used by only one narration beat, so setup and change shots stay distinct.
